questions.q: Why does it matter whether a value is missing at random versus missing because of the value itself (e.g. high earners leaving income blank)?
options: It never matters; every missing value should be handled identically
If missingness correlates with the value itself, the fact that it's missing is informative, and blindly filling or dropping it can throw away a real signal
Random missing values cannot be imputed at all
Only categorical columns can have this kind of missingness
questions.explain: When missingness itself carries information (as with high earners omitting income), simply filling in a typical value erases that signal — which is why a 'was_missing' flag can be worth adding alongside imputation.

questions.q: What does adding a `_was_missing` flag column alongside an imputed value accomplish?
options: It removes the need to impute at all
It gives the model both a usable numeric value and a separate signal that the value was estimated rather than observed
It automatically increases model accuracy in every case
It deletes the original column
questions.explain: The flag preserves the information that a value was missing (which can itself be predictive) while still giving the model a usable number via the imputed value.

questions.q: What's the risk of simply dropping all rows with any missing value?
options: There is no risk; it's always the safest option
It wastes data and can bias the remaining dataset if the missingness isn't actually random
It automatically causes data leakage
It converts numeric columns to categorical ones
questions.explain: Dropping rows loses information and, when missingness correlates with something meaningful rather than being random, can skew the remaining dataset in a way that no longer represents the real population.

questions.q: Why must `SimpleImputer` be fit only on the training split (`fit_transform(X_train)`) and then just applied to the test split (`transform(X_test)`)?
options: Because scikit-learn requires two separate imputer objects
Fitting on the full dataset (including test rows) would let statistics from the test set leak into training, inflating evaluation results
Because the test set never has any missing values
Because transform() and fit_transform() produce different column counts
questions.explain: Just like the fill-value rule from the data cleaning lesson, computing the median (or other imputation statistic) from the full dataset would let test information influence a choice made before training — a form of data leakage.

questions.q: When might dropping an entire column be more appropriate than imputing it?
options: Whenever a column has even one missing value
When the column is missing in most rows, leaving too little real signal to be worth keeping
Only when the column is categorical
Dropping a column is never appropriate
questions.explain: If a column is missing in the vast majority of rows, there may not be enough real information left in it to justify imputing and keeping it, making dropping the column the more reasonable choice.
